        out.write(f'\\n===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n{s}\\n')
        Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i+1}.txt').write_text(s)
print(r.metadata)
print(Path('tmp/pdfs/page-1.txt').read_text())

strengths: Conditional summary graphs provide a useful representation of changing causal interactions. Under the source-specific state assumptions, representing K graphs instead of K^N regime graphs offers a meaningful efficiency advantage. The extension of ACD/NRI through latent states is well motivated.

The controlled particle experiments examine observed, determined, and recurrent states, as well as structures shared across trajectories or varying between them. Near-perfect structure recovery in the fixed-graph experiments provides encouraging evidence that SDCI can recover the intended interactions.

The applications demonstrate potential beyond the particle simulator. On the simulated gene network, SDCI–Determined achieves F1 0.347 versus 0.187 for the strongest baseline by this metric. The NBA results also suggest that adapting interactions can improve forecasting.

The appendices provide substantial architecture, optimization, and data-generation details, together with a code link. The paper appropriately acknowledges that estimator consistency remains unproved and that recurrent states with varying graphs are challenging.
weaknesses: The identifiability argument lacks necessary state-support conditions. In Theorem A.6, the passage from Eq. (35) to Eq. (36) applies Gaussian-mixture identifiability to recover every regime and their total number at a fixed observation history. This only identifies components with positive conditional weight. No corresponding positivity or coverage assumption is stated, and deterministic state assignments generally produce zero weights. An unvisited state with a distinct graph can be added without changing the observation distribution. Consequently, the advertised guarantees, particularly identification of unknown K without restrictions on state dynamics, are not established as stated.

The edge-label proof contains a substantive mathematical gap. Corollary A.8 asserts that permutation invariance makes the aggregator derivatives equal across sources and targets, and independent of the state configuration. A symmetric nonlinear aggregator need not have this property: for g(h)=sum_i exp(h_i), the derivative with respect to h_i is exp(h_i). The implemented aggregator also depends on target features and state-dependent messages. Thus, Eqs. (46)–(49) do not justify a single global permutation of edge types. Stronger assumptions or a different proof are needed for the central theorem.

The claim of exact inference in Appendix B.2 is not justified for the stochastic softmax state model. Even when the state prior depends only on the current observation, subsequent observations inform that state, and shared children couple different source states in the posterior. Therefore, setting q(s_t|x_1:T) to the local state prior is generally an approximation. Equation (57) does not carry out the required joint marginalization, so the claimed exact O(NK) computation needs correction or an explicit deterministic restriction.

The causal-discovery comparisons do not sufficiently isolate the advantage over alternative switching models. Figure 6 primarily compares against methods with fixed causal structures. R-PCMCI appears only in the gene experiment, where Appendix B.4 reports using default settings after tuning encountered problems with short sequences. A suitably configured nonstationary baseline on the controlled benchmarks would make the contribution more convincing.

The gene-network evidence is limited to one 49-gene network configuration. Although the F1 gain is substantial, AUROC is almost tied with Rhino: 0.936 versus 0.933. Threshold-selection details, precision–recall results, uncertainty across training runs, and evaluation across independently generated networks are needed to distinguish improved structural recovery from thresholding or calibration effects. The simulated longitudinal measurements also provide substantially more information than typical destructive single-cell measurements.

The NBA improvement over ACD is small and lacks uncertainty reporting. These forecasts condition on ball features, and the experiment has no causal ground truth; the qualitative graph interpretations therefore offer limited validation of causal correctness. Clarifying future-ball availability and the game-level train/test split would also improve reproducibility. Overall, the empirical promise supports substantive merit, but the unresolved identifiability and inference issues make rejection more appropriate at present.
